newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ricci opens couture season ahead of British revolt.
newsitem.headline: Ricci opens couture season ahead of British revolt.

text.p: Like candy-coated almonds, French designer Gerard Pipart's gowns for Nina Ricci on Saturday gave an artificially sweetened start to a spring-summer haute couture season that promises later to be dominated by British upstarts.

The arrival of Alexander McQueen at Givenchy and John Galliano at Christian Dior -- two of fashions most hallowed names -- is a sign that the erstwhile big guns in Paris fashion are receding into the background as fresh young talent from abroad takes centre stage.

Pipart, attempting to stay in the limelight, showed billowing garden party floral chiffons with over-the-knee hemlines, polka dot Bettina blouses on red and black plaids and frilled and ruffled taffetta tutus.
The mink-swaddled line-up of Nina Ricci's customers, faithful through the decades, squealed with delight as Pipart emerged to take his bows and accepted their bouquet of flowers.
But his inspiration was as lifeless as the artificial birds nestled on the bows in back of a polka-dot evening sheath or in motionless flight around a tulle bridal veil.

Later, Italy's Gianni Versace targetted a younger clientele, layering translucent close-to-the-body chiffon slip dresses in lavender, absinthe, lime and peach florals or motifs inspired by Alexander Calder's mobiles.
"I went in search of lightness," explained Versace in the programme. "Everything that seems weightless, which challenges gravity, fascinates me."

For evening, the chiffon was brushed with gold arabesques on an abstract mix of colours -- pea-green with parma, absinthe and coffee cream, while hemlines fell to the ankles and necklines dipped to the buttocks in back.
Strapless cocktail dresses in quiet navy or lipstick red hugged the body, their slanted hemlines rippling with flamenco-style pleated ruffles.
The Spanish hemline, a constant thread throughout, returned on narrow black skirts paired with ivy-embroidered wool cardigans or on stunning, slinky sheaths in black or ultra-marine blue.
"He took a lot of new directions. It was very interesting in terms of the colours, the new impressions, and the transparencies," said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue

In addition to the much-publicised appointments of McQueen and Galliano, Jean-Paul Gaultier and Thierry Mugler are bringing the experience and cash of their successful ready-to-wear firms to the couture catwalk later this week.
While some members of the small and elite couture community resent the new arrivals as an intrusion on exclusive turf, others feel couture needs new blood.

"The couture is getting a lot more coverage than it ever has before. It will bring new life and eventually a new audience, who may bring new customers. It's creating an excitement and an aura," said Joan Kaner of U.S. department store chain Neiman Marcus.
